title: Book one: debts
hook: Marcus lists what he learned from each person, his grandfather's gentleness, his mother's simple living (Meditations 1.1–3)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the emperor's notebook: Greek notes in a tent by the Danube, written to himself. Your line was to himself. Did you reread your note? Day one hundred sixty-five.

Think about the acknowledgments page at the back of a book. Thanks to my editor, my agent, my partner for putting up with me. Usually we skip it. Now imagine a book that opens with its acknowledgments, and they go on for a whole chapter. And they aren't thanks for help with the book. They're thanks for help with becoming a person. That's how Marcus Aurelius's notebook begins. Before a single piece of advice, he makes a list of the people who shaped him, and what exactly each one gave. Today, book one: debts.
screen: `THE PAGE EVERYONE SKIPS.` → `A WHOLE CHAPTER OF THANKS.` → `BOOK ONE.`

segments.voice: Book one of the Meditations is seventeen short sections, and nearly every one starts the same way: from so-and-so, I learned this. It opens with his grandfather. In George Long's 1862 translation: "From my grandfather Verus I learned good morals and the government of my temper." Then his father, who died when Marcus was small, remembered for modesty and a manly character. Then his mother, and this one is lovely. From her he learned piety and generosity, and to hold back not only from doing wrong but even from thinking it, and, in Long's words, "simplicity in my way of living, far removed from the habits of the rich." Remember who's writing: the richest man in the empire, thanking his mother for teaching him to live simply. The list keeps going. A tutor who taught him to put up with work and want little. A teacher named Rusticus who taught him to read carefully and not be satisfied with skimming, and who lent him the writings of Epictetus. Friends, philosophers, his adoptive father, the gods. Here's what's quietly radical about it. Marcus doesn't start with who he is. He starts with who he owes. Every good habit he has, he traces back to a face. It's the opposite of the self-made man. And notice how specific he is. Not thanks, Mom. Thanks for this exact thing. That precision is the practice. Gratitude gets real when it gets specific. Your line is the question the whole book asks: from whom I learned.
screen: `FROM SO-AND-SO, I LEARNED THIS.` · `GRANDFATHER: GOVERNING HIS TEMPER.` · `MOTHER: SIMPLE LIVING.` · `NOT SELF-MADE: SPECIFIC DEBTS.` · then, large: `FROM WHOM I LEARNED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: list three people and one gift each. Settle, and breathe. Let the first person come: a parent, a grandparent, a coach, a boss, a friend. Now be as exact as Marcus. Not they were great. What, exactly, did they give you? A way of laughing at trouble. Showing up early. How to make soup. Then a second person, and a third. Say each one inside: from them, I learned this. The bell holds the time.
Book one. The opening of the Meditations, where Marcus lists the people who shaped him and exactly what each one gave. Today's word.
Your line: from whom I learned. Today, tell one of your three people, or someone who knew them, the exact thing they gave you. Day one hundred sixty-five.

screen: `DAY 165 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE SONG OF THE REED.`

howItsDone: Many readers of Marcus Aurelius, and many in modern Stoic practice, imitate book one by writing their own list of the people who formed them and the specific thing each one taught.

trapdoor: what you thought: an emperor's list of thank-yous.
what it means: a catalog of specific virtues, each traced to the person who taught it.
what a scholar hears: Meditations 1.1–17, likely among the last parts written; Rusticus (1.7) lent him Epictetus, and 1.16 is a long portrait of Antoninus.
